name: Pang Pema
tagline: Kanchenjunga's north base camp, under a 3,000 m wall of ice
meta_description: Pang Pema, Kanchenjunga North Base Camp at about 5,143 m: the trek from Ghunsa via Kambachen and Lhonak, permits, season, altitude and history.
summary: Pang Pema is the north base camp of Kanchenjunga, at about 5,143 m on the Kanchenjunga Glacier in Taplejung. It faces the mountain's north face across the ice, more than 3,000 m higher. Trekkers reach it from Ghunsa in three to four days via Kambachen and Lhonak, inside the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area.
intro: Kanchenjunga, at 8,586 m, is the third highest mountain on earth, and from most of Nepal it is a distant shape on the eastern horizon. At Pang Pema you are right under it. The base camp sits on a grassy shelf beside the lateral moraine of the Kanchenjunga Glacier, and across the ice the north face rises in a sweep of rock and hanging glaciers to the summit ridge.

Getting here is the reward of one of Nepal's longest and quietest teahouse treks. From Ghunsa the trail climbs to Kambachen, then to Lhonak on a wide sandy plain among moraines, and finally along the glacier edge to Pang Pema. Few trekkers make it this far compared with Everest or Annapurna base camps, and you may have the place almost to yourselves, with only the crack of the glacier and the wind for company.

Most groups sleep at Lhonak and walk to Pang Pema and back in a long day, though some stay a night near the base camp when lodging is available. Either way, it is a serious high-altitude day, and it needs good acclimatisation and settled weather. We build in rest days at Ghunsa and, where needed, at Kambachen, and keep a spare day so the Pang Pema walk can wait for a clear morning.

story.title: The north side of the five treasures
paras: Kanchenjunga was surveyed and admired from Darjeeling long before anyone saw it closely from Nepal, which stayed closed to most foreigners until the 1950s. In 1899 the British mountaineer Douglas Freshfield and the Italian photographer Vittorio Sella travelled around the massif and studied the great western face rising from the Kangchenjunga Glacier, the same glacier that flows past Pang Pema. Sella's photographs of the expedition are still admired today for their detail and scale.

The first ascent came in 1955, by Joe Brown and George Band of a British expedition climbing from the south-west. They stopped a few metres below the true summit, keeping a promise given to the ruler of Sikkim that the top would be left untouched. In 1979 Doug Scott, Peter Boardman and Joe Tasker made the third ascent and the first without bottled oxygen, by a new route on the North Ridge, the side that rises above Pang Pema.

Today Pang Pema is a seasonal camp for expeditions and a goal for trekkers. In spring, climbing teams set up tents on the shelf, with cook tents, prayer flags and a puja altar for the ceremony that opens every climb; in autumn it is usually trekkers only. Herders from Ghunsa and the lower valleys still bring yaks up to the summer pastures around Lhonak, as they have for generations, and their stone huts and walls are scattered across the plain.

legend: People in Sikkim and among the Lepcha tell of a hidden valley of immortality on Kanchenjunga's slopes, a sacred refuge that will open to the faithful in a time of great danger. For Buddhists of the region the mountain is the dwelling of a protective deity, which is why the first climbers stopped short of the summit. Standing at Pang Pema, the stories feel close.
people: No one lives at Pang Pema year round. In the trekking seasons it is visited by guides, porters and lodge-keepers from Ghunsa and the lower Tamor valley, many of them Buddhists of Tibetan descent, along with Limbu, Rai and Sherpa porters and guides from across Taplejung. In summer, yak herders from Ghunsa use the high pastures between Kambachen and Lhonak.

untold.fact: Kanchenjunga was first climbed on 25 May 1955 by Joe Brown and George Band, who stopped just short of the true summit to keep a promise that the top would remain untouched.
In 1979 Doug Scott, Peter Boardman and Joe Tasker made the third ascent of Kanchenjunga, the first without supplemental oxygen, by establishing a new route on the North Ridge.

In 1899 Douglas Freshfield and the Italian photographer Vittorio Sella examined Kanchenjunga's great western face rising from the Kangchenjunga Glacier, one of the earliest close studies of the mountain's Nepal side.

taste.name: Tsampa porridge
taste.text: Roasted barley flour stirred into hot butter tea or milk and eaten as porridge or dough. It is light to carry and quick to cook, which is why herders and porters live on it in the high country. Lodges at Lhonak and Kambachen will make it if you ask.

facts: 3–4 days up via Kambachen and Lhonak

highlights.title: Kanchenjunga's north face
highlights.text: From Pang Pema the north face of the world's third highest mountain fills the view across the glacier, rising more than 3,000 m above the camp. Morning light is best; cloud often builds by early afternoon.

highlights.title: The Kangchenjunga Glacier
highlights.text: The camp sits beside the lateral moraine of the glacier that drains the north-west side of the massif. Walk a short way up the moraine ridge for the full sweep of ice and peaks.

highlights.title: Lhonak's open plain
highlights.text: The night before, Lhonak at about 4,780 m sits on a wide sandy plain ringed by moraines and snow peaks. It feels like a high desert and is one of the most striking campsites in eastern Nepal.

highlights.title: Blue sheep on the slopes
highlights.text: Herds of blue sheep (bharal) graze the grassy slopes between Kambachen and Lhonak, often close to the trail. They are the main prey of the snow leopard, which lives here but is rarely seen.

highlights.title: A base camp without crowds
highlights.text: Pang Pema sees a fraction of the visitors of Everest Base Camp. On many autumn days you share it with a handful of trekkers, and in some weeks with nobody at all.

how_to_reach.text: From Ghunsa (3,475 m) the trail goes to Kambachen (about 4,050 m), then Lhonak (about 4,780 m), then along the glacier edge to Pang Pema, usually as a day trip of 6–8 hours from Lhonak and back. Allow 3–4 days from Ghunsa including acclimatisation, and 2–3 days back.

Reach Taplejung via Bhadrapur or Biratnagar and the Mechi Highway north, then jeeps up the Tamor valley as far as the road is open, and walk from there to Ghunsa. Roads here are changing; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Most trekkers sleep at Lhonak, where simple teahouses have dormitory or twin rooms, a shared toilet and a dining room with a stove, and walk to Pang Pema and back in a day. A basic lodge has operated at Pang Pema itself in some seasons. Kambachen has a few simple lodges. All are very basic and cold, with limited food; a warm sleeping bag is essential. Expedition and camping groups use tents.
tips: Do not rush: spend two nights in Ghunsa and consider an extra night at Kambachen before going to Lhonak.
Start the Pang Pema day at first light; mornings are clearest and you want to be back at Lhonak before afternoon wind and cloud.
Know the signs of altitude sickness and turn back if they worsen; at about 5,143 m Pang Pema is only a little lower than Everest Base Camp.
Carry insurance that covers helicopter evacuation above 5,000 m; it is the only fast way out.
Bring water purification; there is no bottled water to buy at Lhonak or Pang Pema, and plastic is discouraged in the conservation area.

experiences.title: Day trek from Lhonak to Pang Pema
experiences.summary: The goal of the north-side trek: an early start from Lhonak along the moraine of the Kangchenjunga Glacier to the base camp at about 5,143 m, time under the north face, and the walk back to Lhonak.
body: We leave Lhonak at first light, wrapped up against the cold, with breakfast eaten and water bottles filled the night before. The trail follows the lateral moraine of the Kangchenjunga Glacier, gently at first and then with some loose, rocky sections where you need to watch your feet. The altitude makes every step slower; our guide sets an even pace, keeps the group together and calls regular stops for water and snacks.

After about 3–4 hours the trail reaches Pang Pema, a shelf of grass and stones beside the moraine. The north face of Kanchenjunga stands across the glacier, with hanging ice and long ridges leading up to the summit, more than 3,000 m above you. Our guide points out the North Ridge route climbed in 1979 and the peaks around the head of the glacier. Prayer flags left by expeditions flutter on cairns at the edge of the shelf.

We spend as long as the weather and your head allow, usually half an hour to an hour, with hot drinks from a flask and time for photographs. Then we walk back to Lhonak in 2–3 hours, often against a cold afternoon wind. If anyone shows signs of altitude sickness, we turn around early, whatever the distance left. The next day we begin the descent toward Kambachen and Ghunsa, where the air feels rich again.

faqs.q: How hard is the walk from Lhonak to Pang Pema?
faqs.a: It is a strenuous day: 6–8 hours return at 4,780–5,143 m, with loose moraine in places. The height gain is modest, but altitude makes it hard. You need several weeks of trekking fitness and good acclimatisation from Ghunsa and Kambachen.

faqs.q: Can I sleep at Pang Pema?
faqs.a: Most trekkers sleep at Lhonak and visit Pang Pema as a day trip. A basic lodge has opened at Pang Pema in some seasons, and camping groups can tent there. Sleeping at 5,143 m raises altitude risk, so we only plan it for well-acclimatised groups.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Pang Pema?
faqs.a: Pang Pema is usually given as about 5,143 m. Lhonak, the usual overnight stop before it, is around 4,780 m, and Kambachen about 4,050 m. Figures vary slightly between maps and guidebooks, but all of these are serious altitudes that need proper acclimatisation.

experiences.title: Moraine ridge viewpoint above Pang Pema
experiences.summary: For strong, well-acclimatised walkers, a short climb up the slopes above Pang Pema for a wider view of Kanchenjunga's north face, the glacier and the peaks along the Tibetan border, on clear mornings only.
body: From the base camp shelf, a rough path climbs the grassy and rocky slopes to the north. Gaining even 100–200 m opens the view: the full north face of Kanchenjunga, the long glacier curving below it, and the peaks around the head of the valley toward the Tibetan border. The ground is steep and loose in places, and every step at this height takes effort, so we go slowly and stop often to breathe.

We only go up if everyone feels well, the weather is settled and there is time to get back to Lhonak before afternoon cloud and wind. Our guide decides on the spot, and turning back is always an option. Anyone who prefers to stay at the base camp shelf can rest with a member of the team while the others climb. There is no shame in either choice; the view from the shelf is already extraordinary.

It is the best photography spot of the trek, with the whole face and glacier in one frame. Bring a wide lens and keep batteries warm inside your jacket, as cold drains them fast. Gloves thin enough to work a camera help. We spend about twenty minutes at the high point, then descend carefully to the shelf and start the walk back to Lhonak, keeping an eye on the sky.

faqs.q: Is the viewpoint above Pang Pema dangerous?
faqs.a: It is not technical, but it is steep, rocky and high, above 5,200 m. The risks are altitude, cold and slips. We only go up with fit, acclimatised walkers in good weather, and our guide can call it off at any time.

faqs.q: What peaks can I see from Pang Pema?
faqs.a: Kanchenjunga's north face dominates the view, with its long ridges and hanging glaciers. Around the head of the glacier are other high peaks of the massif and the Tibetan border ridge. Your guide will name them on the day.

faqs.q: What time of day is best for photographs at Pang Pema?
faqs.a: Mid to late morning, when the sun lights the face from the side and before cloud builds. Afternoons often bring wind and cloud. In autumn the morning light is usually clear and sharp, while spring mornings can be softer and hazier.

experiences.title: Blue sheep watching between Kambachen and Lhonak
experiences.summary: A slow stretch of trail above Kambachen with time to watch herds of blue sheep grazing the slopes, and a guide who explains the high-altitude wildlife of the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area, from snow leopards to vultures.
body: Between Kambachen and Lhonak the valley opens into grassy slopes and scree, with the river braided across a wide gravel floor. This is good ground for blue sheep, or bharal, which graze in herds and blend into the rock until they move. In autumn the males carry thick, curved horns and the herds are often large. They are surprisingly relaxed around the trail if you stay quiet and keep your distance.

We walk this section slowly, stopping to scan the slopes with binoculars. Our guide explains how the blue sheep fit into the food chain of the high Himalaya as the main prey of the snow leopard, and points out signs such as tracks, scrapes and droppings on the trail. You may also see marmots in summer, pikas darting between stones, and the feeding marks left by herds on the alpine grass.

Snow leopards are almost never seen, but knowing they share the valley changes how you look at it. Lammergeiers and Himalayan griffons often ride the air above, and choughs gather around the lodges. We do not use calls, bait or drones, and we never follow animals off the trail. The aim is simply to walk slowly, look carefully, and enjoy a valley where wild animals still outnumber people.

faqs.q: Where can I see blue sheep on the Kanchenjunga trek?
faqs.a: Blue sheep are often seen on the grassy and rocky slopes between Kambachen and Lhonak, and sometimes near Pang Pema. Early mornings and late afternoons are best, when they move to feed. Binoculars help a lot.

faqs.q: Are there snow leopards near Pang Pema?
faqs.a: Yes, snow leopards live in the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area, but they are very rarely seen by trekkers. You may find tracks or scrapes on the trail. Sightings usually need long, patient watching in winter, when the cats follow blue sheep lower down.

faqs.q: Should I bring binoculars on the Kanchenjunga trek?
faqs.a: Yes, a light pair of 8x or 10x binoculars is worth carrying for blue sheep, birds of prey and the details of the mountain faces. They also help you spot the trail ahead on the moraine.

experiences.title: Expedition history around the Lhonak stove
experiences.summary: An evening around the stove at Lhonak, with your guide telling the story of Kanchenjunga's climbing history, from Freshfield and Sella in 1899 to the 1955 first ascent and the 1979 North Ridge climb above Pang Pema.
body: Evenings at Lhonak are cold and early, and the lodge stove is the place to be. Our guides use the time to tell the mountain's story, and to talk about the porters and climbers from these valleys who have worked on its expeditions. Many families in Taplejung have someone who has carried loads to Pang Pema or worked in a base camp kitchen, and those stories are as much part of the mountain's history as the famous names.

We start with the early explorers, including Freshfield and Sella in 1899, then the first ascent in 1955, when Joe Brown and George Band stopped short of the summit to keep a promise that the top would be left untouched. Then the North Ridge in 1979, climbed without bottled oxygen by Doug Scott, Peter Boardman and Joe Tasker, on the face you will see tomorrow.

It is an informal talk, with questions welcome, and it makes the next morning at Pang Pema mean more. Some guides carry a printed photograph or two of the early expeditions; others draw the routes in the dust or on a napkin. Then it is dinner, usually dal bhat or noodle soup, a last hot drink, and an early night in a warm sleeping bag before the dawn start.

faqs.q: Who first climbed Kanchenjunga?
faqs.a: Joe Brown and George Band of a British expedition reached the top on 25 May 1955, climbing from the south-west, followed by Norman Hardie and Tony Streather the next day. They stopped just short of the true summit to honour a promise that it would remain untouched.

faqs.q: Which side of Kanchenjunga is Pang Pema on?
faqs.a: Pang Pema is on the north-west side, on the Kangchenjunga Glacier in Nepal. The 1955 first ascent was made from the south-west, on the Yalung side. The North Ridge, climbed in 1979, rises above the Pang Pema side.

faqs.q: How high is Kanchenjunga?
faqs.a: Kanchenjunga is 8,586 m, the third highest mountain in the world after Everest and K2. It lies on the border of Nepal and Sikkim in India, and is sacred to many people on both sides. Its massif has five main summits.

faqs.q: What is Pang Pema?
faqs.a: Pang Pema is the north base camp of Kanchenjunga, at about 5,143 m beside the Kangchenjunga Glacier in Taplejung district, eastern Nepal. It is the high point of the Kanchenjunga North Base Camp trek and faces the mountain's north face.

faqs.q: How many days is the trek to Pang Pema?
faqs.a: Allow about 18–22 days from Kathmandu and back for the Kanchenjunga North trek, including travel to Taplejung, the walk to Ghunsa, acclimatisation, the day to Pang Pema and the return. New roads in the lower valleys are shortening it. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Kanchenjunga North trek harder than Everest Base Camp?
faqs.a: It is generally considered harder because it is longer, more remote and has simpler lodges, with fewer chances to rest in comfort or get help. The maximum altitude is similar. It suits trekkers with previous high-altitude experience.

faqs.q: What permits do I need for Pang Pema?
faqs.a: You need the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area permit and a Kanchenjunga restricted area permit, arranged through a registered agency, normally for at least two trekkers with a licensed guide. Since April 2023 foreign trekkers must trek with a licensed guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the best time to trek to Pang Pema?
faqs.a: October and November give the most settled, clear weather. April and May are good too, with warmer days, more cloud and rhododendrons lower down. December to February brings heavy cold and snow, and June to September monsoon rain, cloud and leeches.

faqs.q: Can I combine Pang Pema with Kanchenjunga South Base Camp?
faqs.a: Yes, on the full Kanchenjunga circuit. From Ghunsa, after visiting Pang Pema, the route crosses high passes to Tseram and the Yalung side for the south base camp. It adds about five or more days and needs good weather.

faqs.q: Are there teahouses on the Kanchenjunga North trek?
faqs.a: Yes. Family-run teahouses operate in the villages and at Kambachen and Lhonak, and a basic lodge has operated at Pang Pema in some seasons. They are simpler than in Everest or Annapurna regions, with shared toilets and limited menus.

faqs.q: How do I reach the start of the Kanchenjunga trek?
faqs.a: Fly from Kathmandu to Bhadrapur or Biratnagar, then drive to Taplejung (Phungling) in a long day, or fly to Suketar when flights run. From Taplejung, jeeps go up the valley as far as the road is open. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the altitude risk at Pang Pema?
faqs.a: At about 5,143 m altitude sickness is a real risk. Follow a slow itinerary with rest days at Ghunsa and Kambachen, drink plenty of water, and descend if symptoms worsen. Carry insurance that covers helicopter evacuation above 5,000 m.
